Laser‑Assisted Patterning of Metallized Fabrics for Washable and Durable Electronic Textiles
Muhammad Masud Rana1,2 · Sotoudeh Sedaghat2,3 · Akshay Krishnakumar1,2 · Devendra Sarnaik2,3 · Praveen Srinivasan1,2 · Yashwanth Ramesh1,2 · Md Mahabubur Rahman1,2 · Rahim Rahimi1,2,3

Abstract Wearable electronic textiles (e-textiles) are increasingly being explored for continuous, noninvasive physiological monitoring; however, scalable fabrication of high-resolution circuitry with long-term mechanical and washing durability remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches, including screen printing, inkjet printing, and conductive-thread embroidery, enable the integration of conductive traces into garments but often suffer from limited patterning resolution, binder-related degradation, mechanical instability, and unreliable interfacing with electronic components. Here, we present a selective laser-assisted ablation method for directly defining conductive circuit traces on single-sided metallized fabrics (MFs) composed of woven, multi-stranded silver fiber yarns. This mask-free and chemical-free process enables rapid, digitally programmable patterning while preserving the structural integrity, flexibility, and breathability of the underlying textile. Importantly, localized laser heating simultaneously removes conductive fibers in selected regions and thermally fuses the exposed ends of adjacent silver yarns, thereby suppressing fraying and enhancing the mechanical robustness of the patterned circuit edges. Using a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser tuned for high absorption by silver, controlled ablation at energy densities of 8–26.5 J·cm−2 produced well-defined insulating regions without compromising the conductivity of neighboring traces. Surface and elemental analyses confirmed nearly complete silver removal, with residual silver content below 3% in the ablated areas. The resulting laser-ablated metallized fabric (LA-MF) exhibited low sheet resistance (approximately 2 mΩ/ sq.), retained more than 94% of its initial conductivity after 10000 bending cycles, and maintained stable electrical performance after more than 20 machine-washing cycles. As a proof of concept, a 16-electrode electrical impedance tomography (EIT) array was patterned directly onto the MF and integrated into a compression garment for noninvasive lung-function monitoring. The textile electrodes enabled real-time impedance imaging, and an embedded convolutional neural network accurately classified respiratory states, including normal breathing and breath-hold conditions, even after repeated laundering. This laser-assisted patterning framework provides a robust, scalable, and manufacturing-compatible route for integrating high-performance circuit architectures directly into fabrics for wearable sensing, healthcare monitoring, and next-generation smart textile applications.

Integrated electronics have transformed both daily life and modern healthcare by progressively shrinking sensing, computation, storage, and wireless communication into personal devices that can operate continuously at the point of use [1]. What began with the miniaturization that enabled portable consumer electronics has evolved into body-adjacent technologies, such as smartwatches, fitness bands, smart glasses, patches, and other wearable sensor platforms [2, 3]. scale of this transition is substantial: mobile technologies and services were estimated to contribute about $6.5 trillion, or 5.8% of global GDP, while worldwide wearable-device shipments reached 611.5 million units in 2025 [4, 5]. Within that broader market, wrist-worn devices alone shipped 45.6 million units in the first quarter of 2025, including 34.8 million smartwatches [6]. Beyond their commercial success, these systems have changed how health-related information is acquired by enabling real-time and increasingly continuous measurement of physiological and biochemical signals outside conventional episodic clinical assessment [7, 8]. Wearable sensors are now capable of mining health information in a noninvasive or minimally invasive manner across watches, patches, masks, jewels, and textiles, thereby supporting higher-resolution and longer-duration observation of human physiology in everyday environments [9, 10]. The next major step in this progression is to move electronics from discrete accessories into the garments people already wear every day. Although wrist-worn systems, headmounted devices, and skin-mounted patches have demonstrated the value of continuous monitoring, many of these platforms remain constrained by rigid or semi-rigid architectures and by their limited ability to establish intimate, stable, and spatially distributed contact across large and anatomically diverse body surfaces [9, 11, 12]. Textiles, by contrast, offer softness, breathability, conformability, moisture management, and broad body-area coverage that are difficult to reproduce with conventional thin-film substrates [13–15]. Porous conductive textiles have therefore emerged as especially attractive material platforms for wearable electronics, because they combine electrical functionality with the flexibility, permeability, and wearing comfort expected of conventional garments [16]. For long-duration monitoring, these attributes are not peripheral; they are central to whether a system can be worn naturally and used reliably in real settings [16]. This vision has driven rapid growth in electronic textiles, or e-textiles, in which sensing and electronic functionality are incorporated directly into fibers, yarns, fabrics, or garment assemblies [17, 18]. Textile-based systems have already been explored for electrophysiological monitoring of signals, such as electrocardiography, electromyography, and electroencephalography; for biomechanical and physical monitoring of respiration, pressure, temperature, posture, gait, and sleep; and for biochemical analysis of sweat-borne markers including pH, sodium, uric acid, glucose, lactate, and cortisol [19, 20]. Such capabilities are particularly attractive in contexts where comfort, body coverage, and continuous use matter most, including daily wellness tracking, rehabilitation, and long-term biomedical monitoring [21, 22]. Systematic reviews of biomedical smart clothing further emphasize that the comfort, ease of use, and ubiquity of garments may be decisive advantages for sustained

clinical deployment, precisely because they lower the barrier between sensing technology and ordinary wear [23]. To realize that promise, however, garments must do more than host isolated sensors. They must also contain distributed electrical interconnects that can route signals and power across the textile to measurement sites, connectors, and readout electronics [24, 25]. In practice, this requires circuit traces that simultaneously deliver high electrical conductivity, low mechanical impedance, washability, breathability, and a tactile character consistent with everyday fabrics [25, 26]. Recent reviews of textile electronics identify this integration problem as one of the major barriers to practical systems: textile devices require reliable conductive pathways and connectors, yet the final garment must still remain flexible, lightweight, stretchable, washable, breathable, and unobtrusive [27, 28]. The central challenge in e-textiles is therefore not only the realization of sensors, but also the creation of textile-native circuitry that preserves garment utility while approaching the electrical performance expected from conventional electronics [18, 28]. To date, three principal strategies have dominated the fabrication of textile interconnects [28–30]. The first is based on printing technologies, particularly screen printing and inkjet printing, which adapt conventional graphic and textile manufacturing methods to deposit conductive patterns onto fabric surfaces [31, 32]. In these approaches, a conductive ink or paste containing metallic nano- or microparticles is deposited onto the textile and subsequently dried or cured [32, 33]. Polymeric binders are typically used to immobilize the particles on the rough, porous substrate and to maintain conductive continuity after drying, so charge transport occurs through a percolative network formed between adjacent particles [32, 34]. This route is attractive, because it is low-profile, design-flexible, and compatible with wellestablished large-area printing infrastructure [35]. It also allows conductive features to be added after textile manufacture, which makes it appealing for rapid prototyping and low-temperature processing of sensitive substrates [33, 36]. Despite these advantages, printed textile traces remain limited by the particulate nature of the conductive pathway and by the chemistry required to maintain it. Recent reviews identify oxidative degradation and limited shelf life as persistent problems for metallic inks, especially nanoparticlebased systems, while highly conductive formulations based on silver nanoparticles remain relatively expensive and are not generally known for withstanding the severe washing and wearing conditions expected in garments [37, 38]. Even when printing is successful, practical feature fidelity on textiles is often coarse, because substrate roughness, pore structure, wetting, and ink penetration distort the intended geometry [31]. For example, a recent screen-printing study using conductive pastes on flexible substrates reported that a nominal 1 mm mask produced silver-chloride lines about

1.24 mm wide and carbon lines about 1.36 mm wide [39]. Likewise, a recent washable inkjet study on polyester fabric reported conductive lines in the approximate width range of 209–325 µm, underscoring that the textile substrate still constrains fine-feature reliability even in advanced formulations [38]. In addition, screen-printed textile interconnects often show limited wash and bending durability and frequently require smoothing or encapsulation layers, which adds complexity and can compromise the native tactile and transport properties of the textile [40, 41]. A second widely used strategy relies on conductive yarns, metal filaments, or plated fibers integrated through embroidery, weaving, knitting, or related textile processes. These approaches are attractive, because the conductive elements are introduced through native textile manufacturing routes and therefore preserve, to a greater extent, the softness and deformability of the host fabric [42, 43]. Conductive yarns embedded by weaving, knitting, or embroidery are widely regarded as elegant and unobtrusive candidates for textile circuitry, because they integrate without fundamentally disturbing the textile nature of the system [44]. They also provide more continuous conduction than particle-based inks and can support longer signal paths with electrical behavior closer to bulk-metal transport [45]. However, failure and connection reliability remain major concerns. Studies on conducting yarns under mechanical loading show that bending, shearing, and tension can progressively damage conductive filaments or delaminate metallic coatings, producing unstable resistance and conductivity loss [27, 46]. At the system level, joining technologies remain a persistent problem, and reviews of e-textile connectors emphasize that relatively few solutions have been developed specifically for textile applications. Resolution is also often limited in practical embroidered geometries: earlier embroidery processes using thicker threads reported geometrical accuracy worse than 1 mm, and more recent embroidered structures still commonly exhibit line widths on the order of about 1 mm for linear stitches and roughly 1–5 mm for curved patterns [47, 48]. Although highly optimized embroidery demonstrations can push well below the millimeter scale, those specialized cases do not resolve the broader difficulties of fraying, softto-rigid interfacing, component attachment, and long-term durability under flexing and laundering [49]. A third strategy builds on flexible printed-circuit and microelectronic manufacturing by fabricating circuitry first and then attaching, laminating, or embedding it into the textile. This hybrid route inherits the major strengths of established circuit-board technology, including high routing density, well-defined trace geometry, and conductivity close to that of continuous metals [50, 51]. Encapsulated filament circuits integrated within textiles, for example, have been reported to survive 45 washing cycles and more than 1500 cycles of 90° bending [52]. More advanced direct textile

microfabrication has also recently achieved sub-100 µm metal patterning while retaining permeability and washability [50]. Yet these advantages come with significant trade-offs. Flexible thin-film electronics generally exhibit poorer air and moisture permeability than textiles, which can reduce wearing comfort during long-term use, while direct in-textile photolithography still depends on multistep metallization, resist processing, exposure, development, and etching sequences that remain costly and fabrication-intensive [53–55]. More broadly, reviews of textile-integrated microelectronics note that textile-adapted and textile-integrated approaches still struggle to fully satisfy the simultaneous requirements of flexibility, washability, breathability, and unobtrusiveness needed for practical garments. A practical route forward is therefore to combine the native feel and permeability of textiles with a circuit-definition method that approaches the precision and conductivity of conventional electronics without inheriting the full cost and complexity of photolithography or the electrical limitations of percolative inks [16]. Selective laser processing offers a particularly attractive pathway for this purpose. Laser–matter interactions are inherently wavelengthdependent, and the absorptivity of metals varies with both wavelength and metal type; accordingly, dissimilar material stacks composed of metals and polymers can exhibit strongly different coupling to the same laser beam [56, 57]. Recent reviews further note that pulsed Nd:YAG lasers operating near 1 µm are especially well suited to thin-metal processing because of their efficient coupling and reduced heat-affected zones relative to longer-wave systems [58, 59]. In textile substrates, laser cutting and engraving also provide an important mechanical benefit: synthetic fibers can locally melt at the cut edge, which suppresses unraveling and fraying [60]. These characteristics make selective laser subtraction especially relevant for metallized fibrous substrates, where a conductive surface must be removed with high spatial selectivity while preserving the underlying textile architecture [61, 62]. This concept is strongly supported by prior work on metallized paper. In a foundational comparison of direct and indirect laser ablation of metallized paper, direct Nd:YAG processing at 1.06 µm selectively removed the conductive aluminum coating without damaging the natural fibrous structure of the paper, whereas indirect CO2 processing at 10.6 µm achieved metal removal only through partial substrate etching [56, 63, 64]. Follow-on work then demonstrated one-step laser-induced patterning and sensor formation directly on metallized parchment paper, establishing Nd:YAG processing as a low-cost and scalable manufacturing route for paper-based circuitry and sensing [56, 65]. Building on that foundation, metallized fabrics (MFs) offer a compelling next substrate class. Driven by increasing demand for electromagnetic

2 Results
2.1 Optimization of Laser Processing Parameters

To enable the fabrication of practical and high-performance circuit traces, a systematic study was conducted to identify laser processing conditions that allow selective removal of conductive silver fibers from the MF while preserving the structural integrity of the underlying textile substrate. Achieving this balance is critical for defining conductive pathways with high precision without compromising the mechanical and functional properties of the fabric. A parametric study was performed by systematically varying laser power and scanning speed, thereby generating a range of laser energy densities (J·cm−2). These parameters were organized into a 10 × 10 processing matrix (totaling 100 distinct conditions), enabling comprehensive mapping of the laser–material interaction space. Laser processing was performed along both warp and weft directions to evaluate any directional dependence arising from the anisotropic woven architecture. Analysis of the processed samples revealed four distinct laser–material interaction regimes based on the applied energy density, as summarized in Fig. 2a, b. At low-energy densities (0–1.75 J·cm−2, blue region, n = 20), no significant modification of the metallized surface was observed, indicating sub-threshold conditions insufficient to induce melting or ablation of the silver fibers. At intermediate energy densities (1.8–7.5 J·cm−2, yellow region, n = 37), partial thermal interaction was observed, characterized by localized melting and deformation of the silver fibers without complete removal. In this regime, residual metallic fragments remained adhered to the textile surface, resulting in incomplete electrical isolation. At higher energy densities (8–26.5 J·cm−2, green region, n = 34), efficient and selective ablation of the conductive silver fibers was achieved. Within this regime, the laser energy was sufficient to fully remove the metallic layer, exposing the underlying polyester fibers

while maintaining their structural integrity. In contrast, at excessive energy densities (27–40 J·cm−2, red region, n = 9), the laser-induced thermal load exceeded the tolerance of the textile substrate, resulting in fiber degradation, charring, and partial collapse of the woven structure. These observations establish a well-defined processing window for selective and damage-minimized laser patterning. Notably, similar processing trends were observed for both warp- and weftoriented laser scans, indicating that the ablation behavior is largely independent of fiber orientation despite the inherent anisotropy of the woven structure. To further elucidate the structural evolution across these regimes, representative samples were selected for detailed microscopic analysis at energy densities of 1 J·cm−2 (low-energy), 5 J·cm−2 (intermediate), 10 J·cm−2 (optimal), and 30 J·cm−2 (high-energy), along with pristine MF. Optical microscopy was performed in top-view, edge-view (interface), and cross-sectional configurations, as shown in Fig. 2c. In the pristine MF, all imaging modalities reveal continuous, highly reflective silver yarns with smooth surfaces and uniform filament bundling, tightly interwoven within the textile matrix. Cross-sectional imaging confirms that the conductive silver fibers are confined to the top surface layer, while the underlying polyester fibers form a uniform insulating structure. The polyester fibers exhibit diameters of approximately 7–10 µm, bundled into yarns of approximately 190–220 µm diameter, with consistent interlacing in both warp and weft directions. At low-energy density (1 J·cm−2), the processed samples exhibit minimal deviation from the pristine morphology. Top-view images show slightly reduced surface reflectivity and minor discoloration, suggesting limited thermal interaction. However, no evidence of material removal or structural disruption is observed. Cross-sectional images confirm the absence of melting or deformation in both the silver and polyester fibers, indicating that this regime corresponds to sub-threshold laser exposure. At intermediate energy density (5 J·cm−2), clear signs of thermal interaction with the silver fibers are observed. The silver filaments exhibit localized melting, coalescence, and partial fragmentation, leading to irregular and non-uniform surface morphology. Residual metallic material is frequently observed adhered to the underlying polyester fibers, indicating incomplete ablation. Interface regions display discontinuous separation of conductive pathways, while cross-sectional imaging reveals localized redeposition of molten silver onto the textile substrate. These features suggest insufficient energy for complete removal of the conductive layer. In contrast, at an optimal energy density of 10 J·cm−2, the laser processing results in clean, spatially confined ablation of the silver fibers. Upon entering the optimal processing window (8–26.5 J·cm−2, green region), the sheet resistance exceeded 1 MΩ/sq., effectively reaching the measurement limit of the system and indicating electrical insulation. This behavior confirms complete removal of the conductive silver layer within the ablated regions, while preserving the underlying nonconductive polyester substrate. A similar trend in electrical response was observed for samples processed along the weft direction (Fig. 2d and Fig. S1b), demonstrating that the evolution of electrical sheet resistance with laser energy density is largely independent of processing direction. The consistent behavior across both orientations indicates that laser ablation effectively disrupts conductive yarn networks regardless of their alignment within the woven structure. This behavior is also influenced by the woven architecture and weaving density of the MF, which affect the spacing and interconnectivity of the conductive silver yarn network. Collectively, these results establish a well-defined operational window between 8 and 26.5 J·cm−2, within which selective laser ablation enables complete electrical isolation of patterned regions while preserving the structural integrity of the textile substrate. Additionally, localized thermal effects at the ablation boundaries promote partial fusion of residual silver at fiber ends, which may further enhance mechanical stability by reducing fraying at the edges of patterned conductive traces.
2.2 Reproducibility, Process Robustness, and Patterning Resolution

To comprehensively evaluate the manufacturability of the laser-patterning approach, the reproducibility, robustness to geometric variations, and achievable patterning resolution were systematically investigated. These studies collectively assess the reliability of the process under realistic fabrication conditions and define the practical limits for circuit patterning on MFs.

To determine the achievable patterning resolution and dimensional fidelity under optimal laser processing conditions (10 J·cm−2), a series of test structures with progressively reduced feature sizes were fabricated on the MF. This study enabled evaluation of the minimum trace width and spacing that could be reliably patterned while preserving textile integrity and electrical functionality. Given a laser spot size of approximately 30 µm, selective removal of individual silver yarns (140–150 µm in diameter) was achieved through multiple raster passes (typically 4–5 passes). The achievable resolution is influenced by the woven architecture of the MF, including yarn spacing and interlacing structure, which impose practical limits on feature definition and continuity. Due to the absence of real-time optical alignment and imaging in the laser system, precise positioning of ultra-fine features is limited. Under these conditions, conductive traces with widths of (400 ± 20) µm were reproducibly fabricated without inducing damage to adjacent fibers or disrupting electrical continuity. At this scale, individual yarn pathways can be selectively defined while maintaining mechanical anchoring through localized fusion of adjacent fibers. Microscopic analysis (Fig. S4) confirmed sharp edge definition and spatially confined removal of silver filaments across patterned features ranging from (400 ± 20) to (1200 ± 50) µm in width. pattern fidelity across a range of practically relevant dimensions. Patterning resolution was further evaluated for both warp- and weft-oriented processing (Fig. S5a,b). Conductive traces with widths ranging from 0.4 to 1.0 mm, representative of typical requirements for wearable and flexible electronics, were successfully fabricated in both directions. Electrical characterization revealed the expected inverse relationship between sheet resistance and trace width, consistent with reduced current-carrying cross-section in narrower traces. Notably, only 4–7% variation in sheet resistance was observed between corresponding warp- and weft-patterned traces (Fig. S5c). This minimal variation in electrical performance can be attributed to the uniform distribution and comparable density of conductive silver yarns in both warp and weft directions within the woven architecture. As a result, the effective conductive pathways and electrical transport characteristics remain largely isotropic, leading to consistent electrical behavior irrespective of processing orientation.
2.3 Morphological and Elemental Characterization

The surface morphology and compositional evolution of pristine and LA-MF were systematically investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). These analyses were conducted to elucidate the effects of laser energy density on structural modification and elemental distribution within the MF. SEM micrographs of representative samples processed under four distinct laser energy densities (i) 1 J·cm−2 (low), (ii) 5 J·cm−2 (intermediate), (iii) 10 J·cm−2 (optimal), and (iv) 30 J·cm−2 (high) are presented in Fig. 3a,b. At low-energy density (1 J·cm−2), the silver yarns remained structurally intact, exhibiting smooth filament surfaces, well-defined strand bundling, and continuous metallic coverage along the yarn length (Figs. 3a(i), 3b(i)). No discernible morphological changes or evidence of ablation were observed, confirming that the applied energy was below the threshold required for material removal. At intermediate energy density (5 J·cm−2), partial disruption of the silver filaments was observed. SEM images revealed localized melting, filament deformation, and the formation of irregular agglomerates of resolidified silver redeposited onto the underlying polyester fibers (Fig. 3a(ii)). High-magnification imaging (Fig. 3b(ii)) showed roughened surface morphology and filament coalescence, indicating melt-driven redistribution rather than complete ablation. These features are consistent with insufficient energy input to fully vaporize the metallic layer. In contrast, samples processed at the optimal energy density (10 J·cm−2) exhibited clean and uniform removal of the silver yarns. SEM analysis confirmed complete ablation of the conductive layer, exposing the underlying polyester fibers while preserving their structural integrity (Figs. 3a(iii),

3b(iii)). The exposed fibers retained their original morphology, with minimal surface roughening and no evidence of collapse or thermal degradation. These observations demonstrate highly selective material removal under optimized processing conditions. At high-energy density (30 J·cm−2), the laser–material interaction transitioned from selective ablation to substrate degradation. SEM images revealed extensive thermal damage, including fiber fusion, structural collapse, and loss of the characteristic fibrous architecture (Figs. 3a(iv), 3b(iv)). The resulting morphology appeared as a fused and brittle network with significant deformation, indicating that the applied energy exceeded the thermal tolerance of the textile substrate. To further investigate compositional changes, EDS elemental mapping was performed to analyze the spatial distribution of silver (Ag), carbon (C), and oxygen (O) across the processed samples (Fig. 3c–e). At low-energy density (1 J·cm−2), strong and uniform Ag signals were observed (Fig. 3c(i)), consistent with intact silver yarns. 2.4 Mechanical and Breathability Characterization

To evaluate the effect of laser ablation on the mechanical integrity and structural robustness of the MF, uniaxial tensile testing was performed on dog-bone-shaped specimens processed under a range of laser energy densities. In all samples, laser patterning was confined to the gauge section in order to isolate the influence of the ablated region on the measured mechanical response. Mechanical behavior was evaluated for specimens patterned along both the warp and weft directions of the woven architecture. Figure 4a,b presents representative images of pristine MF and LA-MF processed at 1, 5, 10, and 30 J·cm−2 before and after tensile testing in both warp- and weft-oriented configurations. The fracture morphology provides important insight into the underlying deformation and failure mechanisms of the hybrid textile-metal architecture. In pristine MF specimens, the fracture zone exhibits extensive yarn decrimping, fiber reorientation, and progressive axial elongation prior to failure. At the point of rupture, both the polyester yarns and conductive silver filaments display characteristic frayed filament bundles, fiber pullout, and brush-like fracture ends, indicating a ductile and energy-dissipative failure process. The silver filaments exhibit localized plastic deformation and tensile rupture, while the polyester fibers undergo fibrillation and progressive tensile fracture. Together, these observations confirm that both the polymeric and metallic yarn networks actively contribute to the load-bearing capability of the MF. Samples processed at a low laser energy density of 1 J·cm−2 exhibited fracture morphologies nearly identical to

those of the pristine material. Pronounced fraying, brush-like fiber ends, and progressive filament pullout were observed at the fracture surfaces, indicating that the applied laser energy was below the threshold required to significantly alter either the conductive silver yarns or the underlying polyester structure. At an intermediate energy density of 5 J·cm−2, the fracture morphology changed noticeably. The broken ends of the specimens were dominated by polyester fibrillation, while the characteristic frayed metallic filament bundles were largely absent. This behavior is consistent with partial melting and discontinuity of the silver filaments, which no longer act as continuous load-bearing elements. Residual silver, although still present, appeared as localized molten deposits adhered to the polyester fibers and contributed minimally to tensile reinforcement. A similar fracture morphology was observed in samples processed at the optimized energy density of 10 J·cm−2, where complete removal of the conductive silver layer resulted in fracture surfaces composed almost exclusively of polymer fibers. 2.5 Wash Durability and Reliability Characterization

To evaluate the laundering durability of the LA-MF, changes in electrical performance and structural integrity were systematically monitored following repeated washing under standardized conditions. Straight conductive traces were patterned on MF using the optimized laser energy density of 10 J·cm−2 and subjected to sequential laundering cycles. After each cycle, the electrical resistance was measured to quantify retention of conductive performance (Fig. 5a). For comparison, conductive traces of identical geometry were fabricated on woven polyester fabric using conventional screen printing with a commercial silver paste and exposed to the same washing protocol (Fig. 5b). The LA-MF samples exhibited no visually detectable changes in trace geometry, edge definition, or electrical continuity after repeated laundering. Even after 20 wash cycles, the conductive pathways remained uniform and sharply defined, indicating excellent structural and functional robustness. Optical microscopy further confirmed that the

conductive silver yarns remained mechanically interlocked within the woven textile architecture, with no evidence of cracking, peeling, delamination, or fraying either within the conductive traces or at the boundaries between laserpatterned and non-patterned regions (Fig. 5c). Because the conductive pathways are formed by continuous, multifilament silver yarns intrinsically integrated into the fabric, the conductive network remains mechanically anchored to the underlying polyester substrate and is not susceptible to the interfacial failure mechanisms commonly associated with surface-deposited coatings. Consistent with these observations, the electrical resistance of the LA-MF samples remained highly stable throughout the laundering sequence, varying by less than approximately 5% relative to the initial value after 20 washing cycles (Fig. 5d). Systematic optimization identified an operating window of 8–26.5 J·cm−2 in which complete removal of the conductive layer was achieved with minimal thermal damage to the supporting textile. The resulting LA-MF exhibited low sheet resistance (approximately 2 mΩ/sq.), preserved tensile properties and breathability, retained more than 94% of its initial conductivity after 10000 bending cycles, and maintained stable electrical performance after more than 20 machine-washing cycles. As a proof of concept, the technology was used to fabricate a garment-integrated 16-electrode EIT array for wearable respiratory monitoring. The resulting platform enabled real-time impedance imaging and machine-learning-based classification of respiratory states, while maintaining consistent performance after repeated laundering. These results demonstrate that selective laser patterning of MFs provides a practical and scalable manufacturing approach that combines the electrical performance of continuous metallic conductors with the comfort, permeability, and durability of conventional textiles. Future works should explore on improving patterning resolution through advanced laser systems with real-time optical alignment, extending the methodology to additional conductive textile materials, integrating multimodal sensing and embedded electronics, and adapting the process to roll-to-roll manufacturing for large-scale production.

To demonstrate the practical applicability of laser-assisted patterning of MFs for wearable electronics, a fully textileintegrated electrode array was developed for EIT as a proofof-concept platform for real-time respiratory monitoring. This system highlights the capability of the laser-patterning approach to enable scalable fabrication and seamless integration of electronic functionality into garments for physiological sensing applications. A 16-electrode array was directly patterned onto MF via selective laser removal of the conductive silver fiber layer. The patterned MF was subsequently integrated into a compressive garment designed for close and stable contact with the body. The electrode array was positioned across the anterior abdominal and lower thoracic regions, including both midline and lateral areas, to optimize sensitivity to impedance changes associated with lung expansion and respiratory motion. Each electrode consisted of a laser-defined conductive pathway incorporating a skin–contact interface and an external connection terminal. Electrical connections to the data acquisition system were established using snap-button connectors integrated at the terminal ends, ensuring stable and repeatable electrical interfacing.
